title: The Birth of Impressionism
subject: art
description: In 1874, painters rejected by the Salon put on their own show. A critic mocked Monet and accidentally gave **Impressionism** its name.

hero.hook: One critic's insult, and the first great movement of modern art had a name.

blocks.text: In April **1874**, about thirty artists who had given up on the [[official Paris Salon]] opened a private show in the former studio of the photographer Nadar. Among the canvases, a misty seascape by **Claude Monet** drew the mockery of the critic Louis Leroy.
By making fun of the title *Impression, Sunrise*, Leroy accidentally named the first great avant-garde movement of modern art. Here is how **Impressionism** changed the way we look at the real world.

sections.title: Against the Academy: the scandal of 1863

blocks.text: In the 19th century, art in France obeyed the **Academy of Fine Arts**. At the top sat history painting. Landscape and everyday life counted as minor subjects. To exist at all, a painter had to show at the Salon. The rules demanded precise drawing and a smooth surface, with no trace of the brush.

In **1863**, the jury rejected more than **3,000** paintings. Emperor **Napoleon III** then authorized the **Salon des Refusés**, an exhibition of the rejected works. There the public found *The Luncheon on the Grass* by **Édouard Manet**: a naked woman having lunch with two men in modern dress. The scandal was instant.

blocks.caption: Manet shocks the Salon by mixing a nude with contemporary life

blocks.text: The jurors of the Salon were nicknamed “the firemen”: the ancient warriors in their favorite paintings wore helmets that looked like those of the Paris fire brigade.

Manet refused the soft modeling of the academic painters. He worked in blunt contrasts. Without ever calling himself an Impressionist, he became the face of this [[avant-garde]] that put color ahead of perfect drawing.

The revolution was also a matter of technique. Earlier, a painter ground his pigments in the studio. With [[paint tubes and plein air]] work, he could finally set up outdoors in front of his subject. Out in the wind and the sun, he discovered that the color of an object never stops changing with the hour and the light.

blocks.caption: Monet and his friends paint outdoors to catch the passing moment

blocks.text: Monet sometimes rented a small boat fitted out as a studio, so he could paint from the middle of the Seine, as close as possible to the reflections.

To capture those moments, they laid strokes of pure color side by side. From a distance, the viewer's eye mixes them together. Inspired by the chemist [[Michel-Eugène Chevreul]], they banished black from their shadows and preferred [[complementary colors]]: blue in the shadow of an object lit in orange.

sections.title: 1874: from an insult to a movement

blocks.text: Tired of being turned down by the Salon, the painters of the Batignolles quarter met at the [[Café Guerbois]]. In **1874**, they organized their own exhibition. The group brought together **Monet**, **Renoir**, **Pissarro**, **Degas**, and **Berthe Morisot**, whose talent won through despite the prejudices of the day.

blocks.caption: The photographer Nadar's studio hosts the first Impressionist show

blocks.text: The press was savage. Leroy called them “Impressionists” to say they were only sketches. Yet the group was experimenting in other ways too, helped by [[Japanese prints]], with off-center framing and views from above. The dealer [[Paul Durand-Ruel]] backed them and won over the American market. Between 1874 and 1886, eight exhibitions made a new idea stick: paint your sensation, not a frozen copy of nature.

By claiming that the way of seeing matters more than the subject, the Impressionists opened the road to modern art. Monet would push that logic all the way to the *Water Lilies*, where outlines dissolve and abstraction comes into view. Seurat's [[Neo-Impressionism]] then turned the free brushstroke into a system of dots.

blocks.text: Today these once mocked canvases are among the most visited works in the [[Musée d'Orsay]]. The insult has turned into a triumph.
Born out of a revolt against the Salon in **1874**, Impressionism made light, the free brushstroke, and personal sensation the heart of modern painting.
